property_summary: After any successful fallback call, the contract's balance is zero if block.number is a multiple of 15 (reference) and non-zero otherwise; the mutant transfers on non-multiples, flipping the condition, so it will sometimes leave a non-zero balance after a multiple-of-15 call where the reference would have returned it all.

After a successful fallback call when block.number is a multiple of 15, the contract's balance must be zero in the reference; the mutant incorrectly transfers on non-multiples, so it will have a non-zero balance after a multiple-of-15 call, violating this rule.

For any call sequence to fallback(), the contract's balance must always be exactly the sum of msg.value from all calls minus transferred amounts; the mutant violates this because it allows zero-value calls to trigger balance-draining transfers without contributing 10 ether, breaking the invariant that pastBlockTime is reset and a transfer only occurs after a 10 ether payment.

For any admissible sequence of calls, the contract's balance can only decrease when the caller has previously sent exactly 10 ether; the mutant allows a zero-value call to eventually trigger a balance-draining transfer.

After any call to fallback(), the value of pastBlockTime must be greater than the block.timestamp of the previous call; the mutant allows zero-ether calls, so it can be called more frequently, resetting pastBlockTime without the required delay, whereas the reference requires 10 ether per call, limiting update frequency.
For any call to fallback(), the transaction reverts unless exactly 10 ether is sent; the mutant allows calls with any msg.value to succeed, breaking this strict payment requirement.

After a call to fallback() completes, if the caller sent less than 10 ether, the contract's balance must not decrease; the mutant allows a zero-value call to drain the balance when block.number is a multiple of 15.
After every state-changing fallback call, pastBlockTime must strictly increase (reference); the bug allows it to stay the same, enabling a repeated same-block transfer.

For any two successive fallback calls with the required 10 ether, the reference contract prevents the second call's transfer when block.timestamp equals the previous call's timestamp, while the buggy version allows it.

After any sequence of admissible fallback calls, the contract balance is always 0 if the last call executed at a block number divisible by 15 and the timestamp strictly increased, but the buggy version can leave a non-zero balance when the same timestamp is reused.

For any two distinct calls to fallback with the required 10 ether, if the second call reuses the same block.timestamp as the first, the reference contract prevents the second call's transfer (reverts), while the buggy version allows it and thus can leave a different contract balance after the second call.

For any single admissible call to fallback, if the transfer does not execute for the reference (because of a revert), then the buggy contract will also not execute the transfer, so the contract balance must be equal after the call.
After any fallback call, if the block number is divisible by 15, pastBlockTime must equal block.timestamp; the buggy version leaves pastBlockTime stale.

For any input where the fallback is called with 10 ether and block.number % 15 != 0, pastBlockTime must equal block.timestamp; the buggy version still updates pastBlockTime but does so after the conditional transfer, so the rule holds for both versions — this rule does not differentiate. The actual difference is that in the buggy version, when block.number % 15 == 0, the require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) check uses the old pastBlockTime value since the update is moved after the transfer. The reference always updates pastBlockTime before any transfer, so the check always sees the current block.timestamp against the previous block's pastBlockTime. The general rule is: after two consecutive calls to fallback with 10 ether where block.number % 15 == 0 on the second call, the reference correctly updates pastBlockTime before the transfer, so pastBlockTime == block.timestamp of the second call; the buggy version updates pastBlockTime after the transfer, so pastBlockTime == block.timestamp of the first call, failing the rule.

After two consecutive fallback calls with 10 ether where the block number of the second call is divisible by 15, the reference updates pastBlockTime before the transfer so it equals the second call's timestamp; the buggy version updates pastBlockTime after the transfer, leaving it equal to the first call's timestamp.

In the reference, pastBlockTime is always updated before a transfer, so calling fallback with 10 ether when block.number % 15 == 0 sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp; in the buggy version, the update is moved after the transfer, so pastBlockTime remains the old value, failing the rule that pastBlockTime equals block.timestamp after such a call.

After any sequence of two fallback calls with exactly 10 ether, pastBlockTime must be strictly increasing; the buggy version fails this because it updates pastBlockTime after the transfer, allowing the second call's timestamp check to use a stale pastBlockTime.
